title: Controlled failover test (prod) - readout + next steps
next_steps: Tune trigger windows/hysteresis based on prod test data; propose updated defaults and run a staging re-test before the next prod window
Fix capacity headroom signal staleness and document the authoritative capacity source + ownership
Update dashboards/alerts to separate 'degraded' vs 'failover' and reduce noise from synthetic probes
Revise runbook + comms template with what users actually saw (streaming disconnect patterns, increased tail latency during canary)
Schedule next controlled prod failover window with expanded but still low-risk blast radius (tier/route scoped)
action_items: Miles Thornton - Draft updated trigger policy (thresholds, windows, hold-down timers) and circulate for review - due 2025-04-29
Aisha Bello - Propose burn-rate alert mapping to new failover states (monitor-only vs active) and update alert spec - due 2025-05-01
Harish Reddy - Resolve GPU headroom metric staleness (cache/refresh interval) and validate against fleet source-of-truth - due 2025-04-30
Allison Grant - Update dashboard panels: state transition timeline + customer impact by tier/route; add 'safe-to-failover blocked' breakdown - due 2025-05-03
Connor O'Brien - Update prod enablement checklist (sign-offs, rollback steps, change window notes) and align with on-call approval flow - due 2025-05-02
Tomáš Novák - Runbook edits: add verification steps for streaming + queue drain, and clarify manual override + audit trail lookup - due 2025-05-02
Irene Choi - Confirm DNS/edge TTL strategy for the next test window; document propagation expectations and rollback timing - due 2025-04-30
Mina Haddad - Review progressive failover scoping rules (tier/route/model) and propose simplifications for v1 policy - due 2025-05-01
Felix Schneider - Add audit dashboard linkouts from incident-bot messages and ensure state transitions have consistent IDs - due 2025-05-03
content:
Meeting header
Title: Controlled failover test (prod) - readout + next steps
Date: 2025-04-23 5:05 PM (PT)
Duration: 52 minutes
Organizer: Talia Benson
Attendees (Redwood): Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes, Miles Thornton, Aisha Bello, Tomáš Novák, Mina Haddad, Ethan Park, Irene Choi, Vanessa Ortiz, Harish Reddy, Connor O'Brien, Allison Grant, Sergio Costa, Felix Schneider, Vikram Singh

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- The team reviewed results from the first production controlled failover test (low-risk slice) including trigger behavior, safety-guard checks, routing changes, customer-visible impact, and observability gaps.
- Main issues: trigger detection was slower than expected, synthetic probe noise caused confusing "degraded" flaps, and safe-to-failover capacity gating initially blocked due to a stale headroom signal.
- Progressive failover mechanics worked and rollback was successful, but streaming disconnects and tail latency increased during the canary phase.
- Agreed to tune hysteresis/windows, tighten "degraded vs failed" semantics, improve dashboards/audit trails, and update runbooks/comms before the next production window.

Topics
- Timeline + what actually happened
- Trigger engine performance (thresholds/windows/hysteresis)
- Safe-to-failover checks (capacity + dependency)
- Progressive failover behavior (tier/route scoping)
- Customer impact and SLO / error budget impact
- Observability + incident bot messages + audit trail
- Next test window and rollout gating

Action items (high level)
- Adjust trigger windows/hold-down timers
- Fix capacity headroom signal refresh
- Update dashboards + alerts
- Update runbook + post-test writeup

Transcript

[00:00] Talia Benson: Alright, folks, we’ll get started. This is the readout for the first production controlled failover test. Goal today is, one, shared understanding of what we observed, two, what needs tuning, and three, concrete next steps and next window. This is internal, but we still want it crisp because Neha asked for a short executive recap.

[00:23] Sean Gallagher: Yep. And thank you everyone for doing this without waking up the entire company.

[00:28] Rafael Mendes: (laughs) Yet.

[00:31] Talia Benson: Quick agenda: Miles will do the timeline, Aisha SLO/alerts impact, Mina and Vikram on routing behavior, Harish and Irene on capacity + DNS/edge, then Allison/Sergio/Felix on dashboards and audit, then runbook updates.

[00:47] Miles Thornton: Cool. I’ll share my screen—well, can’t share in Fireflies, but I’m looking at the state transition timeline. The test window was 13:00 to 13:30 PT on Tuesday. We scoped to low-risk slice: hosted API, us-east-1 primary, us-west-2 target, only Tier-3/self-serve traffic, and only chat route group “/v1/chat/completions” pinned to the small set of models in the canary allowlist.

[01:18] Mina Haddad: And importantly not embeddings, and not dedicated.

[01:21] Miles Thornton: Correct. We started in monitor-only at 12:55. At 13:02 we induced partial impairment in us-east-1—packet loss on one path plus elevated 5xx at the edge, basically the same failure mode we saw last quarter.

[01:38] Irene Choi: To be precise, we used the controlled network policy on the edge POP plus a targeted service-level error injection for the gateway.

[01:46] Miles Thornton: Yep. At 13:04 the region health aggregator marked us-east-1 as “degraded” based on the synthetic probes and a 5xx spike, but the trigger engine did not transition to “failover recommended” until 13:10.

[02:04] Aisha Bello: That’s the key delta—our hypothesis was 2 to 3 minutes to recommendation; we got about 6.

[02:10] Miles Thornton: Exactly. Then safe-to-failover checks ran. First run at 13:10:30 was blocked on capacity headroom in us-west-2. It said “insufficient GPU headroom” even though the fleet dashboard showed we were fine.

[02:25] Harish Reddy: It was reading the cached headroom metric from Telemetry, which was lagging by… we think five minutes.

[02:33] Sergio Costa: I saw the same in the panel. It looked like the headroom was red, then suddenly green after refresh.

[02:38] Miles Thornton: Right. At 13:12 safe-to-failover passed after the metric updated. At 13:12:30 the orchestrator moved into “progressive failover: canary 5%” for the scoped slice.

[02:53] Vikram Singh: And that was internal routing policy update, not DNS, in this stage.

[02:57] Miles Thornton: Yes. For the test we intentionally did internal routing first. DNS/edge was in standby, basically.

[03:04] Connor O'Brien: We had the change window pre-approved, and the feature flag gates required on-call approval plus release eng ack. That part went smoothly.

[03:11] Miles Thornton: We held 5% for 7 minutes, then increased to 25% at 13:19, because the canary SLO was within guardrails. Then at 13:23 we observed an uptick in streaming disconnects for that slice. Not catastrophic, but noticeable.

[03:27] Tomáš Novák: Users would see “stream interrupted” and the SDK retry kicks in, right?

[03:31] Vikram Singh: Depending on client. Some clients retry, some just bubble the error.

[03:35] Miles Thornton: Exactly. At 13:24 we paused at 25%. We did not proceed to 50%. At 13:26 we initiated rollback to 0% failover, back to primary, because the impairment was still active and we didn’t want to learn too many things at once.

[03:51] Sean Gallagher: And rollback worked, which is a big win.

[03:54] Miles Thornton: Rollback to 0% completed at 13:27:10. We left the system in monitor-only again. The induced impairment ended at 13:29.

[04:05] Talia Benson: Can you call out what was expected versus what happened, in bullet form?

[04:10] Miles Thornton: Expected: degrade signal at ~13:03, recommendation by 13:05, safe-to-failover passes immediately, canary 5% then 25% then 50% if stable, no meaningful customer-visible issues besides slightly higher latency. Actual: recommendation was late, safe-to-failover was blocked due to stale capacity, and streaming disconnects increased at 25%.

[04:34] Mina Haddad: Also we saw “degraded” flapping from synthetic probes that wasn’t correlated with real customer errors at one point.

[04:41] Miles Thornton: Yep, that happened around 13:06 to 13:08. The aggregator toggled degraded/healthy twice because one probe region timed out.

[04:51] Irene Choi: That probe is running from a POP that was also affected by our test. So we basically shot ourselves in the foot.

[05:00] (crosstalk)

[05:01] Sean Gallagher: That’s actually good learning. We need probe placement guidance.

[05:05] Talia Benson: Great. Aisha, can you cover the SLO and alert behavior?

[05:10] Aisha Bello: Sure. For the scoped slice, we tracked multi-region availability SLO signals and tail latency. During the impairment window, the slice had elevated 5xx on primary, then improved when we shifted 5% and 25% to us-west-2, but latency p95 increased for the canary traffic by about 120 to 180 milliseconds, mostly attributable to cross-region network plus some queueing.

[05:34] Sergio Costa: p99 had a bigger bump.

[05:36] Aisha Bello: Yeah, p99 spiked by ~400ms for a few minutes, then stabilized. Availability-wise, error budget burn: we were still under the “page now” burn-rate threshold because the slice was small, but our alerts were… noisy.

[05:52] Talia Benson: Noisy how?

[05:54] Aisha Bello: We had a “region degraded” alert firing twice due to synthetic probe flaps, and we had a “safe-to-failover blocked” alert firing without enough context. The on-call would have to click three dashboards to understand it was stale capacity data.

[06:10] Felix Schneider: Also the audit events didn’t include the exact metric snapshot used for the decision, just the pass/fail and a reason string.

[06:17] Aisha Bello: Exactly. So for next iteration, I want to align alerts to the failover state machine: monitor-only, recommended, canary, partial, full, rollback. And only page on “recommended” or “active failover” plus burn rate, not on every degraded blip.

[06:35] Sean Gallagher: Plus hysteresis.

[06:36] Aisha Bello: Plus hysteresis, yes.

[06:40] Talia Benson: Mina and Vikram, routing side?

[06:43] Mina Haddad: So progressive failover mechanics worked: policy store updated, propagation to the router fleet happened within—what was it—like 35 seconds average?

[06:53] Vikram Singh: 30 to 45 seconds depending on the cell. That’s within expectation.

[06:58] Mina Haddad: But the scoping logic is a little too complex in config. We had to define by tier plus route group plus model allowlist. That’s okay for controlled tests but for real incidents, we need defaults.

[07:12] Miles Thornton: Agreed. We spent too long double-checking the scoping.

[07:16] Mina Haddad: Another thing: the fallback model variant selection did not engage because the system never entered “degraded-but-available load shed” mode; we went straight from degraded to failover canary. Which is fine, but it means we didn’t validate the graceful degradation controls.

[07:34] Vikram Singh: And there’s an interplay: if you shed load and tighten timeouts in-region, you might not need to fail over. But the trigger engine doesn’t currently consider “mitigations applied” as a factor.

[07:47] Sean Gallagher: We should, eventually. But for v1, I’d rather keep it simple.

[07:52] Rafael Mendes: The other routing note: we saw some sticky sessions causing a few clients to keep hitting us-east-1 even when they were in the canary cohort. That’s due to connection reuse at the edge.

[08:06] Vikram Singh: Yeah, for streaming especially.

[08:08] Tomáš Novák: So that might explain the streaming disconnect pattern?

[08:12] Vikram Singh: It’s a factor. During the shift, some streams got cut because the underlying connection got drained or moved; plus the client was doing long-lived connections.

[08:24] Mina Haddad: We need to clarify what “canary percent routing” means for streaming. It’s not perfectly smooth.

[08:31] Talia Benson: That’s important for comms templates too.

[08:34] Irene, Harish, can you cover infra/capacity and the stale signal issue?

[08:39] Harish Reddy: Yep. So the safe-to-failover check reads: target region GPU headroom, queue depth, and dependency health. GPU headroom comes from the fleet capacity service, but the orchestrator was reading the Telemetry aggregated metric which is updated every five minutes. The fleet dashboard showed headroom was fine because it was near-real-time. So we need to either (a) switch the check to call the capacity service directly, or (b) reduce the telemetry refresh and add a staleness indicator.

[09:07] Allison Grant: Please do (a). The metric pipeline is not for gating decisions.

[09:10] Harish Reddy: I agree. But it’s a bit more work and we need auth and rate limits.

[09:16] Ethan Park: Control plane can provide a signed call path for that, but yeah, it’s non-zero.

[09:22] Irene Choi: On DNS/edge: we didn’t change DNS for this test. But we did validate the plan in parallel. TTL strategy: current TTL is 60 seconds for the relevant health-check records; for enterprise customers it’s sometimes higher due to their own resolvers. For our own edge routing, we can shift within ~30 seconds, but there’s propagation variability. For the next test, if we want to include DNS, we need a longer window and a more conservative rollback plan.

[09:50] Connor O'Brien: And a change window with comms to internal teams; DNS changes always make people nervous.

[09:55] Irene Choi: Right. Also, our synthetic probes—this came up—were running from a POP that we impacted. So the probe failure was not indicative of region health; it was indicative of the test itself. We need guidelines: run probes from at least two unaffected regions and maybe one external provider.

[10:18] Sergio Costa: We can tag probes by source and exclude a source if it’s part of the blast radius.

[10:24] Miles Thornton: That would help for game days too.

[10:27] Talia Benson: Allison, Sergio, Felix—observability gaps?

[10:31] Allison Grant: Main gap is interpretability. The dashboards show raw signals but not decision context. Example: safe-to-failover blocked. You need to know which check failed, the metric value, and how fresh it is.

[10:47] Felix Schneider: Audit trail today logs a transition event like “SAFE_TO_FAILOVER_FAILED: insufficient_headroom,” but it doesn’t include the snapshot—headroom=12% or whatever, timestamp, and what threshold was applied.

[11:02] Sergio Costa: Also, the state timeline panel is hard to read. It shows “degraded” as a single value but doesn’t show flaps or hysteresis windows. We should show the evaluated window and when the hold-down started.

[11:17] Aisha Bello: And align naming. Right now we have “region_health_degraded” in one place and “region_status=yellow” in another. It’s confusing.

[11:27] Allison Grant: Plus, customer impact panels: we had a slice, but the dashboard didn’t show “tier-3 only” clearly. People saw p99 spikes and thought all traffic was impacted.

[11:38] Rafael Mendes: I got DMs about that.

[11:40] Sean Gallagher: Same.

[11:41] Talia Benson: Okay. Let’s talk about what needs tuning in the trigger engine. Miles?

[11:46] Miles Thornton: The big one is detection latency. We used a 5-minute window for tail latency and a 3-minute window for errors with hysteresis requiring two consecutive evaluations. That was conservative to avoid flappy failovers. But in this test it delayed recommendation.

[12:06] Sean Gallagher: Which is fine for now, but our goal is reduced customer-visible impact. Waiting six minutes defeats the purpose.

[12:13] Miles Thornton: Right. Proposal: shorten error window to 90 seconds with a two-of-three evaluation rule, keep latency window longer but make error spikes more decisive, and add a hold-down timer that prevents immediate recovery flaps once you enter recommended.

[12:33] Mina Haddad: What about the synthetic probes? They’re too sensitive.

[12:36] Miles Thornton: I think probes should contribute but not be sufficient alone, at least for “recommended.” Maybe they can drive “degraded” but require customer-impact metrics to escalate.

[12:48] Aisha Bello: I’m aligned. Make probes advisory, not gating.

[12:53] Irene Choi: Or weight them based on source quality.

[12:57] Vikram Singh: Another tuning: dependency health. We only checked the tokenization upstream and one storage dependency. We didn’t check the auth edge path health to target region. If we fail over and auth is unhealthy in target, we can make it worse.

[13:14] Ethan Park: Control plane dependency check can include the auth service health per region. We have that signal.

[13:20] Sean Gallagher: Please add it. I don’t want an unsafe failover.

[13:23] Talia Benson: Let’s capture that as a follow-up; it’s in the action items.

[13:26] Tomáš Novák: For runbook: we also need to add a decision tree: when do you stay in degraded mode with load shedding vs when do you progress to failover. Right now it’s basically “if recommended, you can proceed.”

[13:41] Sean Gallagher: Yeah. But we have to be careful. Too much choice increases on-call confusion.

[13:47] Tomáš Novák: Totally. We can make it prescriptive: “if streaming disconnects > X, pause” etc.

[13:56] Sergio Costa: We can add stop conditions as explicit monitors. During the test, we manually eyeballed the graphs.

[14:04] Rafael Mendes: That was a little stressful.

[14:06] Talia Benson: On customer-visible impact—what did we see in support channels? Tomáš or Rafael?

[14:12] Rafael Mendes: Support didn’t get tickets because slice was small, but in #support there were two internal pings from folks using the platform. The main symptom: streaming dropped and they saw retries. Also tail latency increased for a few minutes.

[14:26] Tomáš Novák: And a couple of “why am I routed to us-west-2?” questions from internal devs who look at headers. So for future tests we should put a banner in #announcements and maybe in console internal banner.

[14:40] Felix Schneider: We can also surface a header like “x-redwood-failover-mode: canary” so it’s obvious. I think we already do, but it wasn’t documented.

[14:50] Mina Haddad: It exists, but only for some routes. We should standardize.

[14:55] Talia Benson: Connor, any release gating issues?

[14:58] Connor O'Brien: Actually, it went well. Approvals were clear. But I want to tighten the checklist: we had 7 different links—dashboard, runbook, feature flag, policy diff, capacity view. For the next window, one doc with everything, plus explicit go/no-go criteria.

[15:18] Sean Gallagher: And ensure the manual override endpoints are permissioned correctly. INT-881 is still open, I think.

[15:24] Ethan Park: RBAC is in progress. Right now override requires the on-call group plus SRE admin. That’s acceptable but we need audit logging for who clicked what.

[15:35] Felix Schneider: Audit has “actor,” but it came through as a service token for two transitions.

[15:41] Ethan Park: Yeah, because the incident bot triggered the state post. We need to preserve user identity through that pathway.

[15:50] Sean Gallagher: That’s important for enterprise assurance too.

[15:54] Talia Benson: Okay. Let’s talk about the streaming disconnects. Vikram, any hypotheses and mitigation?

[15:59] Vikram Singh: Hypothesis: during partial failover, connections get redistributed, and streaming is more sensitive to any mid-stream routing changes or connection draining. Also cross-region adds more RTT, and some clients have aggressive read timeouts. Mitigation: (1) ensure we don’t move active streams; only new requests get shifted, (2) adjust drain behavior, (3) client guidance: recommend timeouts for streaming under failover.

[16:28] Mina Haddad: For (1), we can make routing decision sticky per connection for the duration. But that reduces canary precision.

[16:35] Sean Gallagher: I’m okay with reduced precision if it avoids breaking streams. Reliability > perfect canary math.

[16:42] Aisha Bello: We should encode “streaming disconnect rate” as a stop condition metric. We didn’t have that as a first-class guardrail.

[16:52] Sergio Costa: It exists in logs but not as a clean metric. We can instrument at the gateway.

[16:58] Allison Grant: Please do it in a way that splits client disconnect vs server disconnect. Otherwise it’s noisy.

[17:05] Sergio Costa: Yep, we can tag reasons.

[17:08] Talia Benson: Great. Let’s also hit “flappy failovers” risk. We saw degraded flaps. What’s the plan?

[17:15] Miles Thornton: Two pieces: (1) aggregator will publish a smoothed health score with explicit staleness and confidence, and (2) trigger engine will use hysteresis and hold-down timers so you don’t bounce.

[17:29] Sean Gallagher: And “manual override required” stays for now.

[17:32] Rafael Mendes: For this phase, yes. But we should be explicit: automation can recommend and can execute canary under approval, but not full regional failover without a human.

[17:44] Talia Benson: That matches the risk controls.

[17:47] Felix Schneider: The incident bot message today says “Failover active” even when we were in canary 5%. That’s misleading.

[17:55] Allison Grant: +1. Language should be “Canary failover enabled for X% of scope Y.”

[18:02] Felix Schneider: I’ll fix templates. Also add linkouts: state timeline, policy diff, audit event.

[18:10] Talia Benson: Great. Any open questions from folks?

[18:13] Vanessa Ortiz: I have one on fleet autoscaling. If we do larger scopes, us-west-2 might need to scale up quicker. The capacity check is only checking current headroom, not projected. We should incorporate “burst capacity” readiness.

[18:30] Harish Reddy: That’s true. Right now we can handle +25% for the tested models, but not necessarily +100% for all tiers. We need a capacity plan before expanding scope.

[18:42] Sean Gallagher: This is why we’re doing progressive.

[18:45] Mina Haddad: Also: dedicated customers have pinned capacity. Failover semantics are different. We should keep them out until we have a dedicated-specific plan.

[18:55] Talia Benson: Noted.

[18:57] Aisha Bello: Another question: do we want different triggers per tier? Enterprise tiers are more sensitive.

[19:04] Sean Gallagher: Eventually, but I’d rather not create a matrix of policies yet. We can scope by tier in execution, but keep triggers consistent.

[19:15] Miles Thornton: Agreed. Simpler triggers, controlled execution.

[19:20] Tomáš Novák: On runbook, can we add a “what customers may see” section? Like: “during canary failover, a small % may see higher latency, some streaming reconnects, headers indicating region changes.” It helps support.

[19:35] Talia Benson: Yes, and we’ll align with the comms template.

[19:39] Sean Gallagher: Also we should do a short post in #announcements before next window.

[19:44] Talia Benson: We did last time, but it was maybe too late.

[19:48] Rafael Mendes: And include exact time and what to do if you see issues.

[19:52] Talia Benson: Great.

[19:54] (brief pause)

[19:56] Talia Benson: Let’s go deeper on the detection delay. Miles, do we know which signal held it back?

[20:02] Miles Thornton: It was the tail latency window. Error rate exceeded threshold earlier, but the policy required either error AND latency, or error AND probe failures. Latency p95 didn’t cross until 13:08 because the error injection was somewhat bursty.

[20:22] Aisha Bello: That policy is too strict. In real incidents, error spikes can be enough.

[20:27] Sean Gallagher: Especially 5xx. If 5xx is above X for Y minutes, that’s actionable.

[20:32] Miles Thornton: Agreed. We can make 5xx a primary trigger with a shorter window, with a separate path for latency-only issues.

[20:43] Mina Haddad: But for latency-only, failover might not help; it can add cross-region latency.

[20:49] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. So for latency-only, maybe apply mitigation first, not failover.

[20:55] Vikram Singh: Like tightening timeouts, reducing batch, shedding load.

[21:00] Aisha Bello: Right, which impacts cost/perf.

[21:04] Talia Benson: Okay, that’s a good design thread but maybe not today.

[21:08] Sean Gallagher: We can capture it as “future: mitigations before failover.”

[21:13] Talia Benson: Added.

[21:15] Felix Schneider: On metrics correlation, we don’t have a simple view that overlays “state transitions” with “error budget burn.” We have it in two tabs.

[21:26] Allison Grant: There’s a PR in slo-toolkit for that correlation. But it’s not deployed to prod dashboards.

[21:33] Sergio Costa: We can prioritize. It’s useful for readouts like this.

[21:38] Talia Benson: Great.

[21:40] (crosstalk)

[21:41] Connor O'Brien: Sorry, one more release note: for next prod test, can we require a dry-run in staging within 24 hours prior? Just to ensure nothing drifted.

[21:51] Sean Gallagher: Yes. That should be in the checklist.

[21:55] Talia Benson: Noted.

[21:57] Talia Benson: Let’s do a quick round: one thing that worked well, one thing to improve.

[22:02] Sean Gallagher: Worked: rollback and progressive routing. Improve: speed to recommendation.

[22:08] Rafael Mendes: Worked: human-in-the-loop approvals were clear. Improve: dashboards need a single pane with context.

[22:15] Miles Thornton: Worked: state machine transitions were stable. Improve: policy thresholds; too conservative.

[22:21] Aisha Bello: Worked: we didn’t burn meaningful error budget. Improve: alert noise and naming.

[22:28] Mina Haddad: Worked: scoping did what we intended. Improve: simplify config; streaming behavior.

[22:34] Ethan Park: Worked: RBAC mostly held. Improve: actor identity in audit logs.

[22:40] Irene Choi: Worked: edge/DNS plan validated on paper. Improve: probe placement and excluding test-impacted sources.

[22:47] Harish Reddy: Worked: target region actually had capacity. Improve: make capacity check authoritative and real-time.

[22:54] Connor O'Brien: Worked: change management flow. Improve: consolidate links/checklist.

[22:59] Allison Grant: Worked: baseline instrumentation was enough to debug. Improve: decision context in dashboards.

[23:06] Sergio Costa: Worked: state transition events existed. Improve: metric for streaming disconnect rate.

[23:12] Felix Schneider: Worked: audit trail exists. Improve: include metric snapshots and fix bot message wording.

[23:20] Tomáš Novák: Worked: we followed stop conditions and didn’t push risk. Improve: runbook clarity and comms.

[23:28] Vikram Singh: Worked: routing propagation time. Improve: connection-level stickiness vs canary precision.

[23:35] Talia Benson: Great. Now, next prod window proposal: I’m thinking two weeks, same day/time, but only after we fix capacity check and adjust trigger windows. Does anyone object?

[23:46] Sean Gallagher: No objection, but I want staging re-test first.

[23:50] Irene Choi: And if we add DNS, we need longer notice. But we can keep DNS out for next one.

[23:56] Mina Haddad: Agree—no DNS yet.

[23:58] Harish Reddy: Capacity check fix is required.

[24:01] Talia Benson: Okay.

[24:03] Talia Benson: Also, exec recap for Neha: I’ll draft a one-pager. Sean, can you review?

[24:09] Sean Gallagher: Yep.

[24:10] Talia Benson: Great.

[24:12] (silence)

[24:14] Talia Benson: Any last concerns?

[24:16] Aisha Bello: One more: we should be careful in dashboards not to show “region failed” during test. It triggered some anxiety.

[24:24] Sergio Costa: We can add a “test mode” label when the feature flag is on and scoped.

[24:30] Felix Schneider: And in incident bot message, say “controlled test” explicitly.

[24:35] Tomáš Novák: For on-call training, I’ll do a walkthrough of the new runbook once updated.

[24:40] Sean Gallagher: Good.

[24:42] Talia Benson: Alright, I think we’re good. I’ll send notes with action items and dates. Thanks everyone.

[24:49] Sean Gallagher: Thanks.

[24:50] (call ends in recording shortly after; some participants continue offline)

Notes
- Some transcript timestamps may be compressed; recording continued with minor side discussion but no additional decisions were captured cleanly.
